extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of international journalism; news managers and editors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for how foreign correspondents and foreign news bureaus operate, how they should be staffed and located, and the trade-offs between bureau-based reporting and alternatives (locals, freelancers, parachute journalists, UGC).

rubrics_metrics.name: Insider–Outsider Tension and Rotation Policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign correspondence requires journalists to be insiders and outsiders at the same time; news managers historically rotated postings (usually three years or less) to avoid correspondents becoming too socialized and losing the ability to report 'objectively'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rotation logic: rotating correspondents mitigates perceived loss of objectivity from long postings. Typical historical term lengths were around three years; rotations were also used to reward experienced journalists with desirable postings. The chapter notes obvious flaws with this reasoning and that the emphasis on rotation is contested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local vs Expatriate Correspondent Origin
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically, foreign correspondents were journalists from the same country as their parent organization (often Western-born). More recently, organizations have moved to hire local journalists as correspondents or use part-time local filings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trade-offs: Local journalists bring lived experience and more extensive sourcing networks which can improve understanding and coverage; expatriate correspondents may bring international-affairs training but lack lived experience. Economic motives (locals are cheaper) have driven change. Critics argue reliance on Western correspondents reproduces global dominance and distorts depiction of other countries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of Foreign News Bureaus (Long-term Perspective and Stability)
rubrics_metrics.description: News bureaus are satellite offices set up for newsgathering that offer a long-term perspective on politics, economics and social issues and provide a stable base of operations for journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefits listed: careful city selection (geopolitical/financial/conflict importance), continuity of supporting staff who interpret significance and connect sources, safe base to return to after reporting trips, and capacity to remain in-country for lengthy periods (example: BBC/CNN/AP in Baghdad during 2003 Iraq War). Bureaus enable triangulation and regional sourcing networks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic Placement of Bureaus
rubrics_metrics.description: Bureaus are often established in cities selected for geopolitical importance, financial centrality, or frequent conflicts (examples: Beijing, Brussels, London, Baghdad, Jerusalem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Placement rationale: choosing cities that reflect regional or global significance maximizes ability to cover important developments. The chapter cites a survey listing cities with most bureaus (Brussels, London, Moscow, Rome, New York, Washington, Beijing, Berlin, Madrid) and notes how concentration influences what is reported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supporting Staff Continuity and Roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Supporting staff at bureaus often do not rotate and play important roles in interpreting stories, connecting correspondents with local sources, and offering helpful context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supporting staff provide institutional memory and local links that help correspondents triangulate information and navigate dangerous environments; their continuity partly offsets rotation of foreign correspondents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sourcing Networks and Triangulation Capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Bureaus and long-term correspondents build regional sourcing networks that enable them to get insights from different parts of a country and triangulate information from multiple actors (e.g., Iraqi and Coalition officials).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: outlets with Baghdad bureaus could triangulate reporting during the 2003 invasion. Sourcing depth is presented as a major advantage of bureau-based operations versus short-term or remote coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economics of Maintaining Bureaus
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintaining foreign bureaus is costly — offices, housing, staff salaries, healthcare, education, drivers, translators, security — and these costs have led many organizations to close bureaus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: budget pressures have driven outlets toward cheaper options (freelancers, stringers, part-time locals, parachute journalists) or reliance on global news agencies and aggregation. The chapter emphasizes that budget concerns, not necessarily lack of audience interest, explain much of the decline in bureaus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parachute Journalism and Use of Freelancers/Stringers
rubrics_metrics.description: As bureaus declined, many outlets use freelancers, stringers, and 'parachute journalists' to achieve more 'efficient' newsgathering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implications: Parachute reporting can be cheaper and flexible but may lack the sustained local knowledge, sourcing networks, and contextual depth provided by bureau-based reporters. The chapter links this trend to organizational economics and the decline of full-time correspondents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on Global News Agencies and User-Generated Content (UGC)
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations increasingly rely on global news agencies and aggregation practices that use user-generated content (tweets, Facebook posts, Instagram, YouTube) instead of maintaining expensive bureaus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Risk: While cost-effective, this reliance can contribute to de-professionalization of international journalism and raises concerns about verification, context, and journalistic standards when using UGC as primary reporting sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: De-professionalization Risk
rubrics_metrics.description: The shift toward cheaper newsgathering (UGC, agencies, parachute reporting) is associated with concerns about the de-professionalization of international journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter frames de-professionalization as loss of sustained reporting skills, sourcing depth, and institutional capacity that bureaus historically provided; it is tied to economic pressures and changing organizational practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic Concentration and Coverage Bias
rubrics_metrics.description: The majority of foreign bureaus (and the best-resourced ones) are concentrated in western Europe and the U.S., which contributes to over-representation of news from those countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effect: concentration in certain cities leads correspondents to identify and report stories nearer to where they are stationed, increasing coverage imbalance. The chapter notes this as a structural factor shaping global news agendas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prestige and Organizational Capital of Bureaus
rubrics_metrics.description: Having a good spread of foreign bureaus has traditionally translated into cultural capital for media organizations, indicating resources and commitment to serious newsgathering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizational implication: bureaus were a status symbol and reward for strong journalists; their presence signaled editorial investment in international coverage, which affects newsroom decisions about establishing or cutting bureaus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agenda-setting and Western Dominance Critique
rubrics_metrics.description: Major global journalistic outlets and news agencies (mostly based in the Western Global North) can use their privileged positions to set the news agenda internationally and potentially shape or distort depictions of other countries to align with Western perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical perspective: political-economy framing argues that dominance of Western outlets influences what becomes international news and how regions are portrayed; hiring local correspondents and diversifying staff are discussed as partial responses to this critique.
